title: From a fraud score to a decision
text: Code: github.com/Saminay786/transaction-risk-decision-framework · Status: in progress

title: From a fraud score to a decision
text:
Two transactions, same score
Two card payments arrive at the same moment. One is a €3 coffee. The other is a €900 laptop. The fraud model gives both the same score: a 10% chance of fraud.
The most common rule in fraud tutorials is “decline if the score is above 0.5”. By that rule, both are approved, because 10% is well below 50%.
But look at what’s at stake:

If the coffee is fraud, the bank loses about €3.
If the laptop is fraud, the bank loses €900 plus chargeback fees.

Having an analyst check the laptop costs around €5. That’s clearly worth it. Checking the coffee isn’t.
The same score can call for different decisions. A fraud model tells you how risky something is. It doesn’t tell you what to do about it. This project is about that second step.
Here’s what I found:

Picking the cheapest action for each transaction beats a fixed cut-off. On the test period it cut total cost from €89.8 to €69.4 per 1,000 transactions and stopped 68% of fraud € instead of 49%.
The data is thin, so I report how sure I am. With only 75 frauds in the test window, the saving against the 0.5 rule could be anywhere from −€352 to €3,493 (95% interval). It points the right way, but it isn’t proven yet.
Fine-tuning a cut-off on a few frauds backfired. A carefully tuned two-threshold rule did slightly worse than the plain 0.5 rule on new data.

title: From a fraud score to a decision
text:
Where this started
I first worked on fraud during my Master’s at IIT Madras, on Credit Default and Fraud Risk Prediction (American Express – IIT Madras, 2022). That was a classic modelling project. I cleaned the data, filled gaps with KNN imputation, balanced the classes with SMOTE-Tomek, and compared seven models with stratified K-fold cross-validation. XGBoost won on ROC-AUC and F1.
Looking back, that project stopped at the question “how risky is this case?” A risk team has to go one step further: “so what do we do, and what will it cost?” This project picks up from there.

title: From a fraud score to a decision
section: Three choices, each with a price
text:
Three choices, each with a price
For every transaction, a card issuer can do one of three things. Each choice has a cost if it turns out wrong:








Action
If it’s fraud
If it’s legit




Approve
the bank loses the amount + chargeback fees
no cost


Review (an analyst checks it)
analyst time; most fraud is caught
analyst time + a delayed customer


Decline
fraud stopped
lost sale + an annoyed customer



There’s one more real-world limit: analysts are limited. You can’t review everything, so reviews have to go where they matter most.
That turns the problem into: for this transaction, given its risk and its amount, which action is cheapest, and do we still have review capacity?

title: From a fraud score to a decision
text:
How I built it
The data. I used the public ULB credit-card dataset: 284,807 European card transactions over two days, of which 492 (0.17%) are fraud. The features are anonymised, which suits this project. The interesting part here is the decision, not the features.
Step 1: split by time, like real life. In practice you train a model on the past and use it on the future. So I trained on the first 60% of the timeline, tuned on the next 20%, and kept the last 20% as an untouched test period. Random splits would quietly let the model “see the future”.
Step 2: a plain model, but with trustworthy probabilities. I used LightGBM, a standard choice. The important change from my 2022 project: no SMOTE this time. Resampling helps F1, but it makes the model think fraud is far more common than it is, so a “10%” score no longer means 10%. Here the probability goes straight into a € calculation, so it has to be honest. I checked this with calibration (Platt scaling vs isotonic regression) on held-out data.
Step 3: put a price on each action. With p = fraud probability and A = transaction amount:
cost(approve) = p × (A + chargeback fees)
cost(review)  = analyst cost + p × (share analysts miss) × (A + fees) + (1 − p) × customer delay
cost(decline) = (1 − p) × (lost margin on A + cost of an annoyed customer)
For the laptop at 10%, that gives about €92 to approve, €15 to review, €33 to decline, so it goes to review. For the coffee: €1.80 to approve, more for anything else, so it goes through.
The costs behind these formulas are assumptions I set in one config file: €5 per review, analysts catch 90% of fraud, €15 chargeback fees, 3% lost margin + €10 per wrongly declined customer, €1 delay cost per reviewed legit customer, and reviews capped at 1% of transactions. In a real bank, Finance and Operations would supply these numbers.
Step 4: compare four ways of deciding on the same test period:







Policy
How it decides




P0
approve everything (to see what doing nothing costs)


P1
decline if p > 0.5 (the common default)


P2
two cut-offs, one for review and one for decline, tuned on past data


P3
for each transaction, pick the cheapest action; respect the review cap

title: From a fraud score to a decision
text:
What happened



Total cost per 1,000 test transactions. The black lines show the 95% range from resampling.


Doing nothing (P0) costs €155 per 1,000 transactions. The standard 0.5 rule (P1) cuts that to €90. Choosing per transaction (P3) brings it down to €69.




P1: decline if p > 0.5
P3: cheapest action




Cost per 1,000 transactions
€89.8
€69.4


Share of fraud € stopped
49.0%
68.2%


Fraud € still getting through
€3,941
€2,455


Analyst reviews used
0
33 (out of 569 allowed)



Where does the gain come from? Exactly the coffee-and-laptop situation. P3 spends a few analyst reviews on risky, expensive transactions that the 0.5 rule would have waved through. It needed only 33 reviews to do it, far below the cap.

title: From a fraud score to a decision
text:
Can we trust the gain?
Here the honest answer is “partly”. The test window has only 75 frauds, and a single big fraud can move the totals a lot.
To measure that uncertainty, I resampled the test period 1,000 times and recalculated each time:

P3 is cheaper than approving everything in 99.7% of resamples. That part is solid.
P3 is cheaper than the 0.5 rule in 85% of resamples. That’s encouraging, but the 95% range for the saving still includes zero.

So I wouldn’t present this as “P3 saves €1,162”. I’d present it as a strong case for a shadow pilot: run P3 alongside the current rule, without acting on it, and measure.

title: From a fraud score to a decision
section: A surprise: tuning made things worse
text:
A surprise: tuning made things worse
P2 is what many teams would try first: keep simple cut-offs, but tune them on past data. I tuned them on the validation period, which had only 33 frauds. The best setting it found was “decline above 0.56, never review”. On the test period, that did slightly worse than the plain 0.5 rule.
With so few frauds, tuning mostly fits noise. P3 sidesteps this because it has no cut-offs to tune. It only needs honest probabilities and the cost assumptions. When fraud labels are scarce, which they usually are, that’s a real advantage.

title: From a fraud score to a decision
text:
What if analysts cost more?
The €5 review cost is a guess, so I re-ran everything with review costs from €1 to €20:



How each policy responds as the cost of one review goes from €1 to €20.


P3 adapts on its own. Cheap reviews: it uses more of them (133 at €1). Expensive reviews: it saves them for the riskiest cases (just 4 at €20). Its total cost stays between €67 and €70 throughout, against €90 for the 0.5 rule.
One exception I want to be upfront about: at €1 per review, the tuned P2 does beat P3.

title: From a fraud score to a decision
section: The trade-off a risk leader actually manages
text:
The trade-off a risk leader actually manages
In the end, every fraud policy balances two things: fraud let through and good customers inconvenienced. Plotting one against the other shows where each policy sits:



Fraud € let through vs legit customers reviewed or declined, per 1,000 transactions.


P3 accepts a little more friction (about 0.75 good customers per 1,000 reviewed or declined) to cut fraud let through by about 38% compared with the 0.5 rule. Whether that’s the right balance is a business call. The point is that the chart makes the choice visible.

title: From a fraud score to a decision
text:
What this doesn’t tell us

Few frauds. 75 in the test window, so all the ranges are wide.
The costs are assumptions. Change them and the ranking can change.
Two days of anonymised data. No seasonality, and no card or customer IDs, so the same card could appear in both training and testing.
Instant labels. Here we know right away which transactions were fraud. In real life, chargebacks take weeks to arrive.

title: From a fraud score to a decision
text:
Where it goes next

Apply the same decision layer to the larger IEEE-CIS fraud dataset, split by customer so no one appears in both training and testing.
Simulate delayed labels to see how quickly a policy goes stale.
Estimate how well analysts catch fraud at different risk levels, instead of assuming 90% everywhere.

Back to the coffee and the laptop. A good fraud model gives them the same score, and that’s fine. Its job is to estimate risk. Deciding what to do with that risk is a separate job, and it’s where most of the money is.
The full write-up, with all formulas, the assumptions table and a one-page decision memo, is in the GitHub repo.

title: Promo Optimization Engine
text: Code: github.com/Saminay786/promo-optimization-engine

title: Promo Optimization Engine
text:
The problem
Retailers spend a lot on promotions. The common way to judge them is “units sold during the promo vs. a normal week”. That number mixes up three things: the discount itself, the display or mailer that usually comes with it, and sales that would have happened anyway. Plan from it, and you over-invest in discounts.
The project works through four questions in order:








Step
Question
Method




1. Measure
How much extra volume does a discount actually cause?
Double Machine Learning


2. Decide
Which product should get which discount, in which week?
Integer optimisation (CP-SAT)


3. Cross-check
Does a top-down view agree?
Bayesian marketing mix model


4. Test
How would we prove it works in real stores?
A/B test design: power simulation + CUPED



Data: dunnhumby’s The Complete Journey, with two years of grocery transactions from ~2,500 households plus display and mailer data. I used the 137 top-revenue products over 99 weeks (11,892 product-weeks), excluding fuel, gift cards and miscellaneous items.

title: Promo Optimization Engine
section: 1. Measure: what does a discount really cause?
text:
1. Measure: what does a discount really cause?
I built a product × week panel. The treatment is discount depth. The controls are display/mailer exposure, past sales, seasonality and how much else in the category was on promo. I then estimated the effect with Double ML (EconML LinearDML, LightGBM, 5-fold cross-fitting) and compared it with a naive estimate and a placebo test.




Elasticity θ
What 10% off does




Naive (no controls)
3.49
+42% units


Double ML
2.51 (95% CI 2.18–2.85)
+29% units


Placebo test
0.01
no effect, as expected



About 43.8% of promo volume was non-incremental. Those were sales the retailer would have made anyway.

title: Promo Optimization Engine
text:
2. Decide: build the promo calendar
The per-category effects feed an integer program (OR-Tools CP-SAT). It picks a discount (10/20/30% or none) for each product-week, subject to a budget, weekly promo slots, a frequency cap, a per-category cap and no back-to-back promos. I compared it with a common rule of thumb: deepest discount on the top sellers.
Same $5k budget, 8 weeks, 10 promo slots per week:




Incremental margin
Budget used




“Deepest discount on top sellers”
$60
full


Optimised calendar
$719
37% less



The rule of thumb loses mostly because it puts deep discounts on products that would sell anyway. Treat the absolute dollar figure with caution: step 3 suggests it’s overstated.

title: Promo Optimization Engine
text:
3. Cross-check: the category view
As a top-down check, I modelled weekly category sales for 8 categories with a Bayesian marketing mix model (PyMC-Marketing). It has three levers (discount rate, mailers, displays) and accounts for carryover and diminishing returns.



Margin returned per dollar of retailer discount, by category (Bayesian MMM, 94% credible intervals).



Discount ROI is below 1 in 7 of 8 categories. Soft drinks return about $0.69 per $1 of discount. Only frozen pizza is above break-even (1.24), and even there the interval is wide.
Displays look cheap to break even on (roughly $0.005–0.08 per placement). That hints at moving some discount money into displays, depending on costs I don’t have.
Both models rank the categories the same way. But the category-level effect is only 43–55% of the product-level one for bread, cheese and soft drinks (19% for deli meats). That fits with discounts partly stealing sales from other products in the same category (cannibalisation). So the optimiser’s gain is probably about half what step 2 says.
Model health: 0 divergences, max r-hat 1.008, R² 0.44–0.64 for 7 of 8 categories.

title: Promo Optimization Engine
section: 4. Test: how would we prove it works?
text:
4. Test: how would we prove it works?
A model’s prediction isn’t proof. Before rolling out the calendar, a retailer would want to test it, so I designed the experiment:

Design: randomly split stores 50/50. Treatment stores run the optimised calendar, and control stores keep current practice.
Unit: stores, not shoppers, because a promo calendar applies to everyone who shops in a store. The data has 582 stores. The 137 planned products sell in 115 of them, and 84 have enough weekly sales to include.
Metric: weekly promo margin per store on the planned products.
Analysis: compare the groups with a t-test, using CUPED to adjust for each store’s margin in the 8 weeks before the test. Big stores stay big, so removing that predictable part cuts the noise.

Then I checked the design on real history: 84 stores, with 1,000 simulated tests per scenario.
Is the analysis trustworthy? I ran “A/A tests”: random splits with no real change. The test raised a false alarm 4–6% of the time, which matches the 5% it should.
How big an effect could it detect? I added known lifts to the treatment stores and counted how often the test caught them:



Chance an 8-week test detects a given true lift, with and without CUPED (1,000 simulations each, real store data).










Answer




Smallest lift detectable 80% of the time (8 weeks, CUPED)
≈13% (12% at 12 weeks, 15% at 4 weeks)


Without CUPED
never reaches 80%, even at a 15% lift


Optimiser’s predicted gain vs. current practice
≈3% (≈1.6% if step 3 is right)


Chance of detecting 3% with this test
≈10%


Stores needed to detect 3%
≈1,500



What this means:

With these stores, a test would almost always say “no significant effect”, even if the calendar works. That result shouldn’t be read as the calendar failing.
CUPED matters a lot here. It roughly triples the chance of detecting a real effect.
The real fix is a bigger or less noisy test: full-store sales instead of a 2,500-household panel (here each store sees only ~100 panel households, while a real store likely serves far more), a metric that pools more categories, a longer test, or a switchback design.

It’s much better to learn this before running a test than after.

title: Promo Optimization Engine
text:
Limitations

Observational data. The Double ML estimate is causal only if the controls capture everything that drives both promo decisions and sales.
No cost data. Margin is assumed to be 30% of shelf price, and suppliers are assumed to fund 50% of the discount. Display and mailer costs are unknown.
The optimiser likely over-credits discounts. Cannibalisation is handled only by a simple category cap, and pull-forward (shoppers stocking up) only by a “no back-to-back promos” rule.
The test simulation is simplified. It applies the lift evenly to the store metric, and panel stores only see panel households’ purchases. The method transfers to a real retailer, but the store count doesn’t.
The MMM has 82 weeks per category, and mailers and displays often run together, so their separate effects are uncertain.

title: Promo Optimization Engine
text:
What’s next

Scale the product-level effects by a category-level factor, so the optimiser stops over-crediting discounts.
Model pull-forward directly instead of using a rule.
Extend the test design with a switchback (alternating weeks) and stratified store assignment, and compare their power.
